videos.title: The house is still in Mom's name
videos.hook: Mom passed, and the house is still in her name. Here's why you can't sell it yet.
voiceover: Mom passed, and the house is still in her name. Here's why you can't sell it yet.
In Illinois, a house skips the court only if the paperwork already moved it. A living trust. A transfer on death instrument. Or a deed shared with someone who's still living.
If it was in her name alone, the house usually goes through probate first. Even with a will.
And the small estate affidavit people mention? It doesn't cover real estate.
This week: get a copy of the deed, order death certificates, and keep the insurance paid.
The full answer and a free title guide are at the link.

videos.hook: The federal estate tax won't touch you. Illinois might.

Add up the house, the 401(k)s, and the life insurance. A lot of suburban couples get close.
And in Illinois, a spouse can't use the other spouse's unused four million unless the plan is set up for it.
Run the free estimator at the link to see where you land.

videos.title: How long does probate take in Illinois?
videos.hook: How long does probate take in Illinois? The honest answer.
voiceover: How long does probate take in Illinois?
At least six months for most estates. Creditors get six months from the first published notice to file claims, and that clock can't be sped up.
Simple estates under independent administration often wrap up in about nine to twelve months.
What makes it longer: family disputes, a house that's hard to sell, or heirs nobody can find.
There's a month-by-month timeline at the link.

scenes.text: How long does probate take in Illinois?
Longer with family disputes, a hard-to-sell house, or missing heirs.

videos.caption: Probate in Illinois has a six-month floor. Here's what a typical timeline looks like, and what drags it out.

videos.title: Myth: a notarized will is enough
videos.hook: Myth: if your will is notarized, it's valid.
voiceover: Myth: if your will is notarized, it's valid.
In Illinois, a notary alone doesn't make a will valid. Two witnesses do. They have to watch you sign, and then sign themselves.
And if one of those witnesses inherits under the will, their gift can be cut.
Handwritten will with no witnesses? Illinois doesn't accept it.
Check yours with the free red-flags checklist at the link.

scenes.fact: Illinois needs two witnesses who watch you sign. A notary alone isn't enough.

scenes.text: A witness who inherits can lose their gift.

videos.title: The first bills after a spouse dies
videos.hook: If your spouse just died and the bank froze the account, start here.
voiceover: If your spouse just died and the bank froze the account, start here.
Joint accounts usually pass straight to you. Bring a death certificate and ask the bank to retitle it.
Accounts in your spouse's name alone may need a small estate affidavit or a court order.
Illinois also gives a surviving spouse a separate right to support from the estate. It's called the spouse's award, and it's at least twenty thousand dollars.
Take it one week at a time. The full list is at the link.

videos.hook: If you and your spouse both died tomorrow, who raises your kids? If you're not sure, a judge decides.
voiceover: If you and your spouse both died tomorrow, who raises your kids?
If you haven't named anyone, an Illinois judge picks. Relatives can ask for the job, and they don't always agree.
Naming a guardian in your will tells the court who you want.
Can't agree on who? Score each person on values, location, age, and how they handle money. Lots of couples pick one person for the kids and another for the money.

videos.title: Dementia and no power of attorney
videos.hook: Mom was diagnosed with dementia and never signed a power of attorney. Is it too late?
voiceover: Mom was diagnosed with dementia and never signed a power of attorney. Is it too late?
Not always. A diagnosis doesn't automatically mean she can't sign. If she still understands what the document does and who she's choosing, she may be able to sign now.
If she can't, the family usually needs a court guardianship, which takes longer and costs more.
That's why timing matters. Ask her doctor to note her abilities at the next visit.
There's a free dementia legal checklist at the link.

videos.title: What a TODI does
videos.hook: One form can keep your house out of probate in Illinois.
voiceover: One form can keep your house out of probate in Illinois.
It's called a transfer on death instrument. You sign it, it gets recorded with the county, and you keep full control of your house while you're alive.
When you die, the house goes to the person you named, without probate.
It's not right for everyone. Blended families and people with Medicaid concerns should get advice first.
The full explainer is at the link.

videos.title: Will Medicaid take the house?
videos.hook: Will the state take Mom's house to pay for the nursing home?
voiceover: Will the state take Mom's house to pay for the nursing home?
Here's how it works in Illinois. After a Medicaid recipient dies, the state can file a claim against the probate estate.
But not while a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or disabled child is still living.
And moving the house into your name right before applying can backfire. Medicaid looks back five years.

videos.hook: Myth: you need money to need a will.
voiceover: Myth: you need money to need a will.
A will is less about money and more about who decides. Who raises your kids. Who handles your affairs. Who gets the car and the savings.
Without one, Illinois law decides for you. With a spouse and kids, it's half and half. An unmarried partner gets nothing.

voiceover: If your parents are over 65, make sure these three papers exist.

Two: a power of attorney for health care, so the right person talks to the doctors.
Three: a will or trust, so you know what they want.

videos.hook: Remarried with kids from your first marriage? Your kids might get nothing.

If everything goes to your new spouse, it's theirs. When they die, it goes to their heirs. That might not include your children.
And stepchildren don't inherit from a stepparent by default in Illinois.
A trust can take care of your spouse for life and then pass to your kids.

videos.title: Don't name your kids on life insurance
videos.hook: Don't name your young kids as your life insurance beneficiary. Here's why.
voiceover: Don't name your young kids directly on your life insurance. Here's why.
A minor can't receive the money. In Illinois, a court usually appoints a guardian of the estate to hold it until they turn eighteen, with court reports along the way.
Then at eighteen, it's all theirs, no strings.
Many parents name a trust instead, or set it up under the Illinois transfers to minors law.
There's a free calculator for how much a guardian needs at the link.

videos.hook: Your life insurance payout counts toward the Illinois estate tax.
voiceover: Your life insurance payout can count toward the Illinois estate tax.
If you own the policy, the death benefit is part of your estate. A one-million-dollar policy can push a three-and-a-half-million-dollar estate over the four-million line.
Some families move the policy into a trust so it doesn't count. That has to be done right, and early.

voiceover: Do you have to pay your spouse's credit cards after they die?
Usually not for a card in their name alone, unless it was joint or you co-signed. Illinois can make a spouse responsible for some family expenses, like medical bills, so ask first.
The estate pays valid debts first. If there isn't enough, most unsecured debt goes unpaid.

videos.hook: Myth: if there's a will, there's no probate.
voiceover: Myth: if there's a will, there's no probate.
A will is the set of instructions you give the probate court. It doesn't skip the court.
What actually avoids probate: a living trust, joint ownership with a survivor, a beneficiary form, or a transfer on death instrument.
That's why a house in one person's name usually goes through probate, will or not.

Two. Order several certified death certificates.
Three. Secure the house and the car. Keep the insurance going.
Four. List what the person owned and how each thing was titled.

Where it goes wrong: kids from a prior marriage, a house you want to keep out of probate, a business, or a family member who'll fight.

videos.title: Who decides if there's no health care POA
videos.hook: No health care power of attorney? Illinois law has a list of who decides.
voiceover: No health care power of attorney? Illinois law has a list of who decides.
It goes in order: a guardian, then a spouse or civil union partner, then adult children, then parents, then siblings, and on down.
If three adult kids disagree, that's when it gets hard.
A health care power of attorney lets you skip the list and name one person.

No. Nobody gets them automatically.
Without a will naming a guardian, family members can ask the court, and an Illinois judge decides what's best for the kids.
Two sets of grandparents and an aunt can all ask. That's how custody fights start.
